Manhattan Institute Director of Research Judge Glock suggested on The Alex Marlow Show that historical tort law offers a robust framework for managing AI third-party liabilities.

The Bright Side:
Leveraging existing judicial systems avoids creating expensive new bureaucratic oversight agencies for rapidly evolving technology.

The Breakdown & Plane Error:
Evaluating regulatory strategy through the lens of legal history. Tort law addresses damages after the fact rather than governing technical architectures proactively.

Social Physics Analysis:
This policy stance follows a measured analytical loop, proposing transparent legal accountability rather than opaque federal preclearance mandates.

The Trajectory: The Path of Redemption.
When proposed legal remedies rely on established precedent, it plots a pragmatic trajectory toward judicial arbitration and market adaptation.

The Unavoidable Truth: Established tort law provides clear mechanisms for assigning liability when corporate products inflict harm.

The Unavoidable Lie: Retroactively suing developers solves frontier technological safety risks before they materialize.

Alethekanon:
Traditional legal accountability offers a sturdy baseline, but fast-moving technical risks often outpace retroactive litigation.

Awwthekanon:
It is reassuring to look back at centuries of legal wisdom when navigating scary new technological frontiers.

Suing bad actors after things break is an old playbook, but AI moves so fast judges might need an upgrade too.
